# The AI Business Model Just Collapsed

### And what tech leaders must do right now

In late 2025, I issued frank warnings about AI in a series of posts for premium subscribers:

- On August 8, 2025, I alerted readers to the risk in Meta’s stock —when it was trading at $769 per share. (Since that time, it has fallen 22%.)

- On October 30, 2025, I issued a more emphatic warning of a bubble top, focusing on Meta and Oracle. At that point Oracle was trading at $265. It’s now at $114—a devastating crash of 56%.

- On December 28, 2025, I shifted my attention to data centers and public sentiment, warning that 2026 would witness a huge backlash . I claimed that Silicon Valley was in denial, and that they would get brutally punished on election day in November 2026. That just happened—41 data center initiatives were on the ballot on Tuesday, and 40 of them went against AI.

- In addition, anti-AI candidates won across the board even in states that were perceived as pro-tech. Political experts are shocked by the degree of the backlash, which went beyond anything they had anticipated just a few weeks earlier. But if they had paid attention to the available data, they would know that opposition to AI has been increasing every month—the more people use it, the more hostile they get. The political establishment should have seen this backlash coming a year ago.

- On August 31 of this year, I predicted that “in the next stage, the revolt against AI will come increasingly from inside the tech community.” Just one week later, a number of prominent AI insiders issued public warnings that the technology was dangerous, posing a risk to human survival. Over the course of just a few days, dozens of tech leaders echoed these same concerns.

- Data center stocks have collapsed in the face of the public’s hostility. Consider the case of Coreweave, a super-hot IPO that was trading at $138 when I issued my bubble warning. Today’s it’s down to $42.

I note that each of these articles was fiercely attacked by techies, financiers, and various fellow-traveling bros. They claimed that I was dead wrong, and that my forecasts were ridiculous. One critic even set up a “Ted Gioia Tracking Website”—to measure how poorly I predicted the future.

But the tech community just saw a $2 trillion NASDAQ wipeout in October , and November looks even worse.

Let me emphasize that I’m not here to give stock-picking advice—despite my title, I’m not a real broker. I don’t want anybody to make investment decisions based on my views.

My focus is on something larger, namely the good of society and human flourishing. That’s why I continue to speak frankly on issues of tech over-reach—despite the pushback I get from AI accelerationists.

I wish more cultural institutions and businesses would join me in supporting humans over bots. But that’s not happening—at least not yet. So I will continue to use my small platform to exert a positive impact, as best I can.

As it turns out, the AI advocates would have done well to heed these warnings. They certainly would have lost less money, but they also might have earned the public’s trust—instead of its anger and skepticism.

They still aren’t reading the room. Consider the case of Google, which is trying to bully schools that limit student access to AI.

When they shove AI down the throats of parents and teachers, they are breaking the law—at least based on my reading of the Sherman Antitrust Act, which prohibits companies from using their strength in one product category to force the use of other offerings. But even if they get away with this, they still do irreparable harm to their reputation.

Tech needs to act more responsibly, or government will step in and force their hand. The situation will get worse for them, if they continue to bully and manipulate.

I am not opposed to AI—if it’s handled responsibly. I suspect most of the public feels the same. We’re just asking for a few reasonable protections.

- TRANSPARENCY: Let people know when AI is used. Don’t try to fool them—that just makes them angrier.

- CHOICE: Allow people to opt-in, instead of forcing them to use AI when they don’t want to . That just makes them angrier.

- LEGALITY: Don’t violate copyright law and steal people’s work to train AI. That just makes them angrier.

- RESPECT THE ENVIRONMENT: Don’t build data centers that degrade the environment—forcing them on communities and using political clout to steamroller opposition. That just makes them angrier.

- SAFETY: Stop playing this ugly game of character assassination against people who express safety concerns. The AI elites who claim everybody opposing them is a Chinese operative, are the real rogue operators. They are the source of the actual psy-op. Instead of playing an unconvincing blame game they ought to act like responsible adults—taking safety seriously and implementing reasonable precautions. That’s what every business does, unless it’s hopelessly corrupt. And corruption inevitably makes people angrier.

These are not arduous requests. Just obey the law, tell the truth, and act prudently. The fact that so many corporate leaders resist such basic norms is alarming.

But it’s also the reason why they are getting hammered right now—in the stock market, the voting booth, courts of law, and the larger court of public opinion.

Let me add a few specific requests—consider this my holiday wish list for 2026:

- To Spotify and major record labels: Stop enabling slop, and support human artists instead. That’s what the fans want and what the culture deserves.

- To Google: Let people connect to the web and outside creators, instead of turning every search request into an AI query. Take a look at your own subsidiary YouTube for some tips on how to support creators and users, instead of just manipulating them.

- To Microsoft: Don’t keep pushing AI on customers unless they explicitly opt-in. Listen to your users—they will guide you better than your corporate yes-men.

- To Amazon: Get rid of the slop that’s flooding your product offerings. You got rich off authors and the book business, so why are you now working to destroy them?

- To social media CEOs: Clean up the slop on your platforms, and make them friendly to actual human beings. Stop punishing links to outside creators—those are essential to a flourishing online community.

- To all corporate CEOs: Before you replace customer service with AI bots, ask your customers how they want to be served. That’s the whole point of customer service, isn’t it?

- To teams managing web platforms: Embrace transparency and honesty. Don’t keep promoting slop as if it’s human work. Don’t empower scammers. Instead of forcing AI and algorithms on everyone, give users some control over their interface.

- To colleges, publishers, non-profits, media and other culture organizations: Stop dawdling, and find a spine. You need to put people first. We are looking for you to show some leadership, not sit on the sidelines.

Tech leaders can still turn the tide, and win public support. But not without adjusting their agenda. They really have no choice—and time is running out.

If they continue to rely on brute force tactics, the backlash will grow worse. If they thought 2026 was bad, wait until they see what happens in 2027 and 2028.
